pr_title: dns: default to verbatim=true in dns.lookup()
pr_body:
Switch the default from false (reorder the result so that IPv4 addresses
come before IPv6 addresses) to true (return them exactly as the resolver
sent them to us.)

Fixes: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/31566
Refs: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/6307
Refs: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/20710

Reissue of https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/31567
pr_comments: @nodejs/tsc ... do we need to to take the current default through a deprecation cycle first?
This could use a test
The failing tests look like they're just wrong assertions that `localhost` resolves to `127.0.0.1`.
Yeah, now the question is...should `localhost` resolve to `127.0.0.1`, or should `assert` test for `::1`? I prefer the latter, but I see good reasons for the first one as well.
The test should simply assert that it's one or the other, allowing either, since the result you get depends on whether the environment is ipv6-capable.
Is there an OR statement for `assert.strictEqual`?

> Is there an OR statement for `assert.strictEqual`?

You can use assert.match and a RegEx.

I suspect it's failing now because the debugger only listens on `127.0.0.1`:
https://nodejs.org/en/docs/guides/debugging-getting-started/

Now, either we assume that every IPv6 system will always be reachable via IPv4 at least on localhost, we could change `localhost` to hardcoded `127.0.0.1`. Or is it possible that the debugger listens on dualstack localhost? I am not sure that is supported.

I feel lilke one problem here is that instances are listening on `127.0.0.1` by default and the documentation doesn't really give clear instructions on how to solve this and about the notation of IPv6 addresses (e.g. with or without braces); or if `::` means IPv6-only or `INADDR_ANY`. Or is `0.0.0.0` euqal to `INADDR_ANY`?

Another obstacle will be to make the code really dualstack. Because `localAddress` can't hold a hostname. Exchanging `127.0.0.1` by `::1` is probably causing issues on legacy IPv4-only systems? So I see lots of `if/then/else` coming. I'll definitely will need some help there. So suggestions very welcome.

> about the notation of IPv6 addresses (e.g. with or without braces);

I think we don't need to add `[]` for apis in `net` module as it's for **ipv6 in url**, see: [rfc2732](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2732).

```
net.isIP('[::]') // return 0 so `net` module will regard it as a pipe socket.
```

@treysis Are you problems you described in the test framework or the actual runtime?

FYI `INADDR_ANY` is `0.0.0.0` and `::` is the IPv6 any address but binding to it can normally accept IPv4 connections as well unless the OS or local policy blocks doing so. (And some people have strong opinions over this one way or the other.)

> I think we don't need to add `[]` for apis in `net` module as it's for **ipv6 in url**, see: [rfc2732](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2732).

I know. But I couldn't always understand from the code if it is handled this way. E.g. it seems like sometimes the code uses some assumptions about IPv6, thus `http://<ip>:<port` might work if ip=IPv4, but for IPv6 it should be `http://[<ip>]:port`, simply speaking.

> @treysis Are you problems you described in the test framework or the actual runtime?

It seems the actual runtime works fine. It is the test framework that fails and thus the `verbatim=true` cannot be merged. That was the problem of the previous PR.

> FYI `INADDR_ANY` is `0.0.0.0` and `::` is the IPv6 any address but binding to it can normally accept IPv4 connections as well unless the OS or local policy blocks doing so. (And some people have strong opinions over this one way or the other.)

You're of course right (INADDR_ANY vs. INADDR6_ANY). I think the test framework should work dualstack. So binding to both `0.0.0.0` and `::` should be the way to go. Yet sometimes the test framework code requires definite IP addresses, e.g. for `127.0.0.1`, and there's no _address_ that equals both `127.0.0.1` and `::1` at the same time. And `localhost` doesn't work, because an IP address is required. Not sure how this can be solved.

Of course I'd be fine if we just expect IPv6 to be working so whoever has it disabled and runs into problems with the test framework -> fix it yourself.

> Of course I'd be fine if we just expect IPv6 to be working so whoever has it disabled and runs into problems with the test framework -> fix it yourself.

You can skip the test if IPv6 is not available:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/b149eefa82327af9835d3c68b3fd03e0e4a25413/test/async-hooks/test-graph.http.js#L4-L5

An even better solution would be to fallback to IPv4 though:

```js
const localhostIP = common.hasIPv6 ? '::1' : common.localhostIPv4;
```

BTW, if you want to expose that as `common.localhostIP` in `test/common/index.js`, I think that would make sense.

> BTW, if you want to expose that as `common.localhostIP` in `test/common/index.js`, I think that would make sense.

I'm not that well versed in JS. Would you mind writing up a few lines of code and I'll happily add it to the PR?
I'll add it after the end of the current test run :)

It's building fine now. However, my local copy fails (maybe firewall? But why firewall when connecting to `::1`?).

Solved it. The issue was that the system resolved `localhost` to `127.0.0.1` first, which was used when binding the listen socket of the inspector. I changed my system to resolve `localhost` to `::1` first, and now the tests are passing. Should this somehow be handled? Maybe more `localhostIP` instead of dualstack? Seems like dualstack isn't even supported and it will listen only to either `127.0.0.1` or `::1`.

Why are the tests depending at all on what "localhost" resolves to and whether it's IPv4 or v6 or matches whether the host has IPv6 capability?! Just use "::1" where you mean ::1, "127.0.0.1" where you mean 127.0.0.1. I wonder if there's a reason why the string "localhost" should ever appear at all - is it just an allergy to "magic numbers"?

Because that is what the `verbatim`-option is causing. After setting it to `true`, some tests would fail because they resolve `localhost` differently now, giving precedence to IPv6 (at least on most systems). The idea about listening on `localhost` was to use dualstack, which is apparently not working. It's either listening on `127.0.0.1` or `::1`, but not both.
Also, hardcoding IP addresses is a bad idea as it will cause problems in the future when a host might not have IPv4 connectivity at all. Although that might be irrelevant for the test suite.
In the end, it should be up to the OS to determine to use either IPv4 or IPv6. So yeah, we can hardcode `::1` and `127.0.0.1` everywhere, but that's just gonna cause even bigger difficulties in the future.

But this is the tests, not the actual code, and the tests are not trying to test the resolver or the verbatim option, just stuff that happens to involve accessing a local server. They already have hard-coded references to 127.0.0.1 and ::1 in them and it doesn't make sense to me to *mix* that with references to "localhost". Using one or the other uniformly, and never trying to assert that the lookup of "localhost" produces a particular address, would be a lot less fragile.

In general, hardcoding either `::1` or `127.0.0.1` is a bad idea. Even for the test suite. Maybe there'll be one day with a test system that doesn't have IPv4; or just somebody running the tests on his system without IPv4, maybe even completely without IPv4 stack.

Thank you for your distinct review @aduh95. However, I don't think it will work with your suggestions. The problem is that we can't predict what `localhost` resolves to, as usually assuming `127.0.0.1` just worked fine. However, it also seems NodeJS differs what it resolves to in `.listen` and `.connect`. Also, this is additionally related to system settings and local resolver. E.g. on my Linux Mint, `ping localhost` would only resolve to `127.0.0.1`, because DNS server is not really used for `localhost` and instead looked up in the `/etc/hosts`, where `::1` isn't specified for the `localhost` hostname by default. However, using systemd-resolved might do it's own 'magic' for localhost. As might 'dnsmasq'.
I.e., there's still too much heterogeneity. As long as `localhost` was reliably resolving to `127.0.0.1` no matter if dualstack or not, this wasn't a problem. But now it is. And with `verbatim=true` by default, NodeJS will usually return `::1` for `localhost`.

All the same, the test suite needs some good reworking to make it ready for real dualstack operation. And since NodeJS doesn't do Happy Eyeballs and only listens on single sockets, we need to make a lot of assumptions and workaround. That should all go in a separate PR. It should probably also involve some fixtures of the CI nodes. Most seem to have been addressed, and actually it seems only SmartOS doesn't resolve `localhost` to `::1` when connecting. But the tests should also all work on systems that don't have IPv6 at all (though I wouldn't mind breaking on systems that turned IPv6 off).

To keep it simple and clean, I suggest to leave this PR as it is, with the fixes for hardcoding to assume IPv4 where it is necessary. Once this is done we can work on the test suite.

Finally, it would be great if we can land this PR in v16 to be supported in the coming LTS to aid global IPv6 adoption.

I understand not all my suggestions are going to work, and it's definitely OK to dismiss them. However I'm confident there are still valid ones (or rather, valid concerns), if you could take the time to comment on each of them explaining why you prefer not to take it, that'd help this PR land.

review_comments:
The inspector should "just work" with the default IMHO, the fact that it defaults to IPv4 goes a bit against that. I think it comes from here: https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/f392ac0bbe3f3757872b9c7cdc785928034b62e9/src/node_options.h#L85
Not that it has anything to do with this PR, I just wanted to point it out.
It should, but it doesn't. On some systems it will listen on `127.0.0.1`, and on others it will listen on `::1`.

We can try this but I think it's safer to use hardcoded IPv4 because not specifying the host would mean it defaults to `localhost` anyways which was always expected to be `127.0.0.1` by the test suite.

Instead of doing this, I suggest changing line 62 to
```js
server.listen(0, common.hasIPv6 ? '::1' : '127.0.0.1');
```
That way, we are still testing the default value.

I don't think that works. Or we have to change the connect-line as follows as well:
`client = net.connect(address.port, common.hasIPv6 ? '::1' : '127.0.0.1', function() {`

Otherwise it will listen on `::1` on an IPv6-enabled system, but will try to connect to `127.0.0.1` and will fail with `ECONNREFUSED`.

> Otherwise it will listen on `::1` on an IPv6-enabled system, but will try to connect to `127.0.0.1` and will fail with `ECONNREFUSED`.

Hum that's not what I see on my machine… It tries to connect to `::1` as expected.
If you don't specify a host in `net.connect`, it will use `localhost`, which always resolves to `127.0.0.1` with `verbatim` set to `false` (that's the current test). With `verbatim` set to `true`, it will resolve to `::1` on IPv6 enabled system, and to `127.0.0.1` otherwise.

Anyway, I don't feel strongly about this, if you think it's simpler let's keep IPv4 for this test.

It did almost everywhere. But on SmartOS it would still resolve to `127.0.0.1`, probably because `::1 localhost` is not set in `/etc/hosts`. I seem to remember that it also resolved to `127.0.0.1` on my machine until I set that line in `/etc/hosts`. This wasn't a problem because the Linux kernel always adds `127.0.0.1` to the `lo`-interface, so even on an otherwise IPv6-only system it would still have that `127.0.0.1` address available and most software will not only listen on `::1` but also `127.0.0.1`. Until we can be sure that every system will also have `::1 localhost` I think the safe solution is to hardcode the address here.

> Until we can be sure that every system will also have `::1 localhost` I think the safe solution is to hardcode the address here.

One could argue that the safe thing to do is to keep `verbatim` to `false`… If it's not easy to fix our CI machines, I don't think we can expect our users to fix their machines when updating Node.js.

I'm sure if we add `::1 localhost` to `/etc/hosts/` will solve this. Unfortunately I don't have access to SmartOS to examine this. As mentioned already, IPv6 is here to stay and should be accounted for. Having systems with faulty IPv6 will fail eventually. This is a bit ideologic, though, I have to admit. But landing this in the next LTS would give people both the time and the incentive to fix some fundamental issues. Otherwise people that need IPv6 will suffer. Unless we rewrite a lot of the logic, to catch all all cases, and/or implement dualstack listeners (for `localhost` at least) this could cause some tiny problems. And those will only affect `localhost`.

Instead of doing this, I suggest changing line 52 to
```js
server.listen(0, common.hasIPv6 ? '::1' : '127.0.0.1', common.mustCall(function() {
```
That way, we are still testing the default value.

That is problematic because we don't know if `localhost` resolves to `::1` or `127.0.0.1`. And that will be the default as it seems if we don't specify the `host` for `http.get`. If we do as per your suggestion, we should also do
```
host: common.hasIPv6 ? '::1' :  '127.0.0.1'
```
I think it's better to stick to pure IPv4 for now.
